title: Trump Lights a Diya in the Oval Office as Governors Mark Diwali Across the US
excerpt: President Donald Trump hosted a Diwali celebration in the Oval Office on Friday and was gifted a Hanuman Chalisa, while governors from Washington to Nebraska issued proclamations honouring Indian American contributions, ANI reported.
body:
• President Donald Trump hosted a Diwali celebration in the Oval Office on Friday, lighting a diya and receiving a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa from entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, ANI reported.
  • Governors in Washington, Nebraska, North Dakota, Idaho and Montana marked Diwali with proclamations and celebrations honouring the Indian American community, according to ANI.
  • Washington Governor Bob Ferguson signed a proclamation declaring November 8, 2026, as Diwali, the Festival of Lights Day in Washington State.
  • White House Diwali observances date to 2003 under George W. Bush; Barack Obama became the first sitting president to personally light a diya at the White House, in 2009.

From state capitals to the Oval Office, senior American leaders marked Diwali this year with what ANI described as a resounding affirmation of the cultural, economic and civic contributions of the Indian American community. The centrepiece was a Friday celebration inside the Oval Office, where President Donald Trump lit a traditional diya ahead of the festival's observance on Sunday.

The Oval Office celebration

The White House's official schedule listed the gathering for 1:30 p.m. EST in the Oval Office, without press access. Among those present were India's Ambassador to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, FBI Director Kash Patel and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, according to ANI and The Daily Jagran. Micron Technology chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna, chef Vikas Khanna and Deputy Commissioner of the Social Security Administration Arjun Mody also attended.

Entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, founder of GOQii, presented the president with a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa, the devotional hymn to Lord Hanuman. Gondal wrote afterwards that he was honoured to celebrate Diwali with Trump and that he had prayed for enduring ties between India and America.

"Honoured to celebrate Diwali with President @realDonaldTrump and proud to gift him a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa, Tulsidas's hymn to Lord Hanuman that millions of us recite for courage, devotion and strength."

— Vishal Gondal, entrepreneur, on X

Governors from Washington to Nebraska

In Washington State, Governor Bob Ferguson praised the state's demographic makeup while officially commemorating the holiday. "We are proud to be home to one of the largest shares of Indian Americans in the country, and we have seen this community contribute so much to our state," Ferguson said, according to ANI. "So, with that in mind, I was proud to sign a proclamation declaring November 8, 2026, as Diwali, the Festival of Lights Day here in Washington State."

In Nebraska, Governor Jim Pillen emphasised the cultural alignment between the celebrations and regional values. "The Indian community is an incredibly vital piece of who we are as the people of Nebraska," Pillen said, closing with the line that gave ANI's report its headline: "Never, ever, ever let the light go out." North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong underscored the ties binding the regions together, and Idaho Governor Brad Little and Montana Governor Greg Gianforte also marked the festival, ANI reported.

A tradition since 2003

White House Diwali observances trace back to 2003 under the administration of George W. Bush, when ceremonies were mostly held in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, The Hindu BusinessLine noted. In 2009, Barack Obama became the first sitting US president to personally light a ceremonial diya in the White House, during a ceremony in the East Room. Since then, lamp-lighting ceremonies have been held in various rooms of the White House, including the Oval Office and the Roosevelt Room.

For the diaspora reader, the through-line of this year's observances is geographic spread. Diwali proclamations and capitol celebrations are no longer confined to states with the largest Indian American populations; governors in Nebraska, North Dakota, Idaho and Montana — states where Indian American communities are smaller but growing — used the festival to put that presence on the official record.
